passage:
Age five: when Lalit's small friend dropped his ice-cream cone and wailed, Lalit's own lip trembled and tears ran down his face, though his cone was fine. He pushed it into the boy's hand. 'You have mine.' Then, frowning, he asked his father, 'Why am I crying?'

Age fifteen: their classmate Diya came out of the audition room in tears. Chetan felt it like a stone in his own chest, his eyes stinging, but he stood frozen, unable to find a word. Beside him, Kamal read the situation like a page. 'She practised for weeks, and she's afraid she let everyone down.' He said it calmly, then checked his watch, unmoved. Later Chetan learned to ask 'What would help?' and Kamal learned to sit down next to her.

Age twenty: in the hostel, Lalit was everybody's listener. One night he heard three friends' troubles until two, skipped his own assignment and snapped at his roommate the next morning. Lying awake, he saw that he had been carrying everything. Next time a friend brought a crisis he said, 'I care about this. I can listen for half an hour, and I will give you the counsellor's number, but I can't fix it for you.'

qa.q: What did Lalit say as he pushed his cone into his friend's hand?
qa.a: 'You have mine.'

qa.q: How do the three scenes show different sides of empathy?
qa.a: At five Lalit cried because his friend cried, feeling with him but not yet keeping the feeling separate. At fifteen Chetan felt Diya's pain deeply but froze while Kamal understood her clearly but stayed unmoved, and at twenty Lalit's caring overloaded him until he set limits.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling as Diya came out in tears?
qa.a: Deep sympathy and helplessness, a stone in his chest with no words to offer.

qa.q: What limit did Lalit set, and how does it help?
qa.a: He offered half an hour of listening and a counsellor's number while saying he could not fix it, so he can keep caring without wearing himself out.

grounding: Empathy across five, fifteen and twenty: catching a friend's tears, feeling versus understanding, and caring until overloaded.

passage:
Age two: Charu jammed the star-shaped block at the round hole again and again, her lip pushed out. Twice she threw it on the floor and then picked it up again. Her father did not take it from her. He steadied the box with one hand and gently turned the block a quarter. Click, it dropped. Charu clapped and shouted, 'I did it!' and looked at his face for the cheer.

Age five: Tenzin frowned at a jigsaw of a farm, one sky piece still missing, arms crossed over his chest. His aunt Pooja reached toward the table. 'Don't tell me!' Tenzin said. Pooja sat back and folded her hands in her lap. After a while she said, 'Try the corner with the red barn.' Tenzin bent over the corner, found the piece in seconds and grinned so widely that his cheeks bunched up. 'I did it myself.'

qa.q: Which corner did Pooja suggest to Tenzin?
qa.a: The corner with the red barn.

qa.q: How did each adult support the child's win without taking it, at two and at five?
qa.a: Charu's father steadied the box and turned the block a little so she could finish it, and Pooja only suggested the corner with the red barn. Each child still felt the win was their own

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when the block dropped?
qa.a: Proud and delighted, as her clapping and her look at her father's face show.

qa.q: What could Pooja do if the nudge is not enough?
qa.a: Offer a slightly bigger hint, such as which two pieces might fit, and still leave the placing to Tenzin.

grounding: A toddler and a preschooler each succeed just past their current skill with a small adult hint that leaves the win their own.

passage:
At fifteen, Kunal was made class monitor. By the second week he was writing names on the board for anyone who whispered, telling classmates to fetch his water bottle, and laughing when they grumbled. When Irawati said, 'You never listen when we ask for a change,' he waved her off. 'Rules are rules.' He liked the sound of his own voice carrying across the room.

At twenty-one, Kunal was head of the hostel cultural committee. A first-year, Noor, asked to swap her rehearsal slot because of an exam. 'Not my problem,' he said, scrolling through his phone. That afternoon he moved his own group into the better slot 'just this once'. A senior passing by said, 'You've changed, you know.' Kunal blinked. 'No, I haven't,' he said, and meant it.

qa.q: Who asked to swap a rehearsal slot because of an exam?
qa.a: Noor, a first-year.

qa.q: How did Kunal's use of authority show the same pattern at fifteen and at twenty-one?
qa.a: Both times he enjoyed being obeyed, waved off a complaint from Irawati or Noor, and bent things his own way, first by bossing classmates and then by taking the better rehearsal slot. At twenty-one he did not notice the change.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he said, 'No, I haven't'?
qa.a: Sure of himself and unaware of the change, so the senior's remark surprised him.

qa.q: What could Kunal do to check his own behaviour?
qa.a: Ask a friend to say honestly how he treats juniors, and listen to complaints like Irawati's before dismissing them.

grounding: The same person's small authority at fifteen and larger authority at twenty-one bring bossiness, less care for others' views and bent rules.

passage:
Age two: Yogesh's mother asked, 'Where is your bear?' and waited. Silence. Two seconds. Four. Then he toddled to the bed and pointed under the pillow. 'Bear.' She had not repeated the question once.

Age ten: asked whether he had seen who broke the class plant, Karthik looked at the floor. 'Um... I don't know.' The teacher did not accuse. 'Take your time. Are you unsure, or is something worrying you?' After a moment Karthik said, 'Someone told me not to tell. I don't want to get them in trouble.' The teacher nodded. 'Thank you for telling me. Let's work out how to handle it fairly.'

Age fifteen: Trisha texted her friend at six in the evening and heard nothing until ten. She typed three angry drafts and deleted them. Then she wrote, 'Hey, did I say something? You went quiet.' The reply came fast: 'Sorry! Cricket practice, then my phone died 😅'

qa.q: How long did Trisha's friend take to reply?
qa.a: From six in the evening until ten.

qa.q: What can a pause mean at two, ten and fifteen, and what did the listeners do?
qa.a: Yogesh's mother waited through the silence and he found the bear. Karthik looked at the floor, and the teacher asked what was worrying him instead of accusing. Trisha's friend replied late because of practice and a dead phone, so she asked and did not guess

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as he hesitated?
qa.a: Worried about getting someone in trouble, torn between telling and protecting them.

qa.q: What could Trisha do next time a reply is late?
qa.a: Ask directly and kindly, as she did, rather than guessing that she has been rejected.

grounding: Pauses read at two, ten and fifteen: a toddler's thinking delay, a child's worried hesitation, and a late text reply.

passage:
At twenty, Neelam had slept badly, skipped lectures and stopped answering messages for five weeks. She kept telling herself it would pass. When she could not finish an assignment she had once loved, she went to the campus counselling centre that same afternoon with her roommate beside her. The counsellor listened, said it was good she had come, and booked a first session for the next day.

At twenty-five, Payal wanted help with constant exhaustion and knotted thoughts. She checked that the psychologist she found held a licence, and after two sessions she felt she was not being heard, so she tried another, who suited her better. When she began to feel better, she kept her appointments instead of stopping. One night her friend Lalit told her on the phone that his own thoughts of hurting himself frightened him. Payal stayed on the line, asked whether he was safe right then, and they rang the helpline together. When he said he wanted someone beside him, she called his neighbour, who took him to the emergency department, and Payal stayed on the phone until staff met him there.

qa.q: How many sessions did Payal have with the first psychologist before trying another?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: How do Neelam's and Payal's experiences show when and how to seek help?
qa.a: Neelam went to the campus counselling centre after weeks of poor sleep, skipped lectures and a stalled assignment. Payal chose a licensed psychologist, switched for a better fit and kept her appointments, and she treated Lalit's frightening thoughts as a crisis for the helpline and emergency care rather than waiting.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling on the phone that night?
qa.a: Frightened by his own thoughts of hurting himself, and needing someone close.

qa.q: Why was staying on the line and ringing the helpline a sound response for Payal?
qa.a: It checked that Lalit was safe right then and brought trained help straight away instead of waiting until morning.

grounding: Signs that it is time to seek help at twenty, and choosing qualified help and using a helpline and emergency care in a crisis at twenty-five.

passage:
At fifteen, Rekha visited her cousins in another state. Asked where the bus stop was, she pointed with her whole hand. The neighbour lifted his chin toward the road instead and frowned at her hand. 'Where I come from, we don't point like that,' he said, and then they both laughed. Rekha tried again: 'Down the road, second lane, next to the tea stall.' The neighbour nodded. From then on she added words to every gesture.

At twenty-six, Jatin held up his hands on a video call to show a part about the size of a small box. The screen froze mid-gesture and half his hands were cropped. Samir, who had joined from another office, frowned. 'Bigger than a shoebox?' Jatin shared his screen and drew the size on a slide. 'Roughly this, fifteen centimetres.' 'Now I see it,' said Samir.

qa.q: What did the neighbour do instead of pointing with a hand?
qa.a: He lifted his chin toward the road.

qa.q: How do both scenes show that a gesture can mislead, and what did each person add?
qa.a: Rekha's whole-hand point looked odd to a neighbour who pointed with his chin, so she added words and landmarks. Jatin's hand shape was cropped and delayed on camera, so he shared a slide with the size drawn on it.

qa.q: What might the neighbour have felt when Rekha pointed?
qa.a: Surprised, or a little put off by a point that seemed rude where he lives, though the shared laugh shows it stayed friendly.

qa.q: What could Samir do the next time a gesture is unclear on a call?
qa.a: Ask for the size in words or a quick sketch instead of guessing.

grounding: Descriptive gestures that mislead across regions at fifteen and on video calls at twenty-six, fixed by adding words and visuals.
